t.E213.agn: In 2016 EFSA set a combined acceptable daily intake (ADI) for benzoic acid and its salts of 5 mg/kg body weight, expressed as benzoic acid; it stated that this limit may be exceeded in young children who consume a lot of the same brand, particularly from flavoured drinks. When present together with vitamin C (ascorbic acid), small amounts of benzene may form in drinks; the FDA monitored this issue and manufacturers adjusted their formulations.
t.E213.eff.0.t: The daily limit may be exceeded, particularly from flavoured drinks
t.E213.eff.0.w: Young children who consume a lot of the same brand
t.E213.eff.1.a: Even at low amounts below the daily limit
t.E213.eff.1.t: Sensitivity reactions such as hives, itching, runny and blocked nose have been reported; in these people it may trigger asthma and eczema symptoms. Anaphylaxis has been reported in a single case
t.E213.eff.1.w: Some people with atopic dermatitis, chronic hives, itching or persistent rhinitis
t.E213.eval: Benzoates may form benzene in drinks containing vitamin C (ascorbic acid) (benzene is IARC Group 1); the industry therefore adjusted its formulations. The mixtures in the Southampton study also contained sodium benzoate, but the EU does not require a separate warning label for this substance.
t.E213.prod: Produced by chemical synthesis; benzoic acid also occurs naturally in some fruits.
t.E213.pw.0: According to EFSA, the daily limit may be exceeded in young children who consume a lot of the same brand.
t.E213.regx.0: Re-evaluated; combined ADI for benzoates 5 mg/kg (as benzoic acid).
t.E213.summary: The calcium salt of benzoic acid. Used as a preservative in acidic foods.
t.E213.what: Extends shelf life by delaying spoilage caused by microorganisms; works best in acidic products.
